claim: KCNQ5, KCNN4, and KCNK5 potassium channels positively modulate cationic CPP direct translocation into cells by decreasing the transmembrane potential (Vm).
source: Using a CRISPR/Cas9-based screening, we discovered that KCNQ5, KCNN4, and KCNK5 potassium channels positively modulate cationic CPP direct translocation into cells by decreasing the transmembrane potential (Vm).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPR/Cas9 screening data presented in the manuscript, which identified these specific potassium channels.

claim: CPPs, by bringing positive charges on the outer surface of the plasma membrane, decrease the Vm to very low values (–150 mV or less), a situation coined megapolarization that triggers formation of water pores used by CPPs to enter cells.
source: In silico modeling and live cell experiments indicate that CPPs, by bringing positive charges on the outer surface of the plasma membrane, decrease the Vm to very low values (–150 mV or less), a situation we have coined megapolarization that then triggers formation of water pores used by CPPs to enter cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by both computational modeling and live cell experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Megapolarization lowers the free energy barrier associated with CPP membrane translocation.
source: Megapolarization lowers the free energy barrier associated with CPP membrane translocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by metadynamics simulations showing reduced free energy barriers at -150 mV compared to 0 or -80 mV.

claim: The diameter of the water pores in living cells was estimated to be 2 (–5) nm.
source: Using dyes of varying dimensions in CPP co-entry experiments, the diameter of the water pores in living cells was estimated to be 2 (–5) nm, in accordance with the structural characteristics of the pores predicted by in silico modeling.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-entry experiments with propidium iodide and dextrans of different sizes, as well as computational modeling.

claim: Pharmacological manipulation to lower transmembrane potential boosted CPP cellular internalization in zebrafish and mouse models.
source: Pharmacological manipulation to lower transmembrane potential boosted CPP cellular internalization in zebrafish and mouse models.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments using valinomycin to hyperpolarize cells in zebrafish and mice.

claim: TAT-RasGAP317-326 sensitizes cancer cells to chemo-, radio-, and photodynamic therapies.
source: TAT-RasGAP317-326 sensitizes cancer cells to chemo-, radio-, and photodynamic therapies (Chevalier et al., 2015; Michod et al., 2009; Pittet et al., 2007; Tsoutsou et al., 2017) and prevents cell migration and invasion (Barras et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: TAT-RasGAP317-326 exhibits antimicrobial activity.
source: This peptide also exhibits antimicrobial activity (Heulot et al., 2017; Georgieva et al., 2021; Heinonen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: Raji, SKW6.4, and HeLa cancer cell lines are directly killed by TAT-RasGAP317-326.
source: Some cancer cell lines, such as Raji (Burkitt's lymphoma), SKW6.4 (transformed B-lymphocytes), and HeLa (cervix carcinoma), are directly killed by this peptide (Heulot et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous published work.

claim: TAT-RasGAP317-326 accesses the cell's cytosol by direct translocation through the plasma membrane.
source: The peptide first accesses the cell's cytosol by direct translocation through the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing cytosolic localization of the peptide and is part of the mechanism described in the manuscript.

claim: TAT-RasGAP317-326 binds to phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylinositol-bisphosphate enriched in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: It then binds to specific phospholipids, such as phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylinositol-bisphosphate that are enriched in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mechanistic description provided in the manuscript and cited work.

claim: TAT-RasGAP317-326 binding to specific phospholipids allows the peptide to disrupt the cell's membrane causing death by necrosis.
source: This binding allows the peptide to disrupt the cell's membrane causing its death by necrosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mechanistic description provided in the manuscript.

claim: Most CPPs can enter cells by direct translocation and by endocytosis.
source: Most CPPs can enter cells by direct translocation and by endocytosis (Bechara and Sagan, 2013; Futaki et al., 2013; Guidotti et al., 2017; Illien et al., 2016; Jones and Sayers, 2012; Koren and Torchilin, 2012; Madani et al., 2011; Mueller et al., 2008; Ruseska and Zimmer, 2020; Trabulo et al., 2010; Vasconcelos et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous published work.

claim: TAT-RasGAP317-326 enters cells via endocytosis and direct translocation.
source: This is also the case for TAT-RasGAP317-326 (Figure 1A–B and Videos 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing both vesicular and cytosolic staining patterns.

claim: The cytosolic acquisition of TAT-RasGAP317-326 occurred only through direct translocation and not through endosomal escape.
source: In our experimental settings, the cytosolic acquisition of TAT-RasGAP317-326 occurred only through direct translocation and not through endosomal escape (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Video 4) and was not due to phototoxicity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) as can occur in some settings (Dixit and Cyr, 2003; Ha and Tinnefeld, 2012; Levitus and Ranjit, 2011; Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse experiments showing no increase in cytosolic signal after washing out the peptide, and by experiments showing that illumination frequency does not affect internalization.

claim: TAT-RasGAP317-326 enters cells via endocytosis and direct translocation, but only direct translocation mediates its biological activity and leads to cell death.
source: TAT-RasGAP317-326 enters cells via endocytosis and direct translocation, but only direct translocation mediates its biological activity and leads to cell death (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing correlation between high intensity fluorescence (indicative of direct translocation) and cell death.

claim: KCNQ5 was identified in Raji cells as a voltage-dependent potassium channel.
source: KCNQ5, identified in Raji cells, is a voltage-dependent potassium channel.
evidence: This claim is based on the CRISPR/Cas9 screening results and established knowledge about KCNQ5.

claim: KCNN4 identified in SKW6.4 cells is a calcium-activated channel.
source: KCNN4 and KCNK5, identified in SKW6.4 cells, are calcium-activated channels and belong to the two-pore (voltage-independent) potassium channel family (Shieh et al., 2000), respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on the CRISPR/Cas9 screening results and established knowledge about KCNN4, with a citation.

claim: KCNK5 identified in SKW6.4 cells belongs to the two-pore (voltage-independent) potassium channel family.
source: KCNN4 and KCNK5, identified in SKW6.4 cells, are calcium-activated channels and belong to the two-pore (voltage-independent) potassium channel family (Shieh et al., 2000), respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on the CRISPR/Cas9 screening results and established knowledge about KCNK5, with a citation.

claim: XE-991 fully blocked TAT-RasGAP317-326 internalization in Raji cells and protected them from the killing activity of the peptide.
source: The KCNQ family inhibitor, XE-991 (Schroeder et al., 2000), as well as KCNQ5 genetic invalidation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), fully blocked peptide internalization in Raji cells and protected them from the killing activity of the peptide (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced internalization and cell death in the presence of XE-991.

claim: KCNQ5 genetic invalidation fully blocked TAT-RasGAP317-326 internalization in Raji cells and protected them from the killing activity of the peptide.
source: The KCNQ family inhibitor, XE-991 (Schroeder et al., 2000), as well as KCNQ5 genetic invalidation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), fully blocked peptide internalization in Raji cells and protected them from the killing activity of the peptide (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced internalization and cell death in KCNQ5 knockout cells.

claim: SKW6.4 cells individually lacking KCNN4 or KCNK5 were impaired in their ability to take up TAT-RasGAP317-326 and were partially protected against its cytotoxic activity.
source: SKW6.4 cells individually lacking KCNN4 or KCNK5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), or SKW6.4 cells treated with TRAM-34, a KCNN4 inhibitor (Wulff et al., 2001; Wulff et al., 2000), were impaired in their ability to take up the peptide and were partially protected against its cytotoxic activity (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced internalization and cell death in knockout cells.

claim: TRAM-34 treatment of SKW6.4 cells impaired their ability to take up TAT-RasGAP317-326 and partially protected them against its cytotoxic activity.
source: SKW6.4 cells individually lacking KCNN4 or KCNK5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), or SKW6.4 cells treated with TRAM-34, a KCNN4 inhibitor (Wulff et al., 2001; Wulff et al., 2000), were impaired in their ability to take up the peptide and were partially protected against its cytotoxic activity (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced internalization and cell death in TRAM-34 treated cells.

claim: Inhibition of KCNN4 activity with TRAM-34 in KCNK5 knock-out cells did not further protect the cells against TAT-RasGAP317-326-induced death.
source: Inhibition of KCNN4 activity with TRAM-34 in KCNK5 knock-out cells did not further protect the cells against TAT-RasGAP317-326-induced death.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing no additional protection when both channels are inhibited.

claim: In HeLa cells, TRAM-34, but not XE-991, inhibited TAT-RasGAP317-326 internalization and subsequent death.
source: In HeLa cells, TRAM-34, but not XE-991, inhibited TAT-RasGAP317-326 internalization and subsequent death (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing differential effects of the two inhibitors in HeLa cells.

claim: In HeLa cells, KCNN4 channels regulate the membrane translocation of TAT-RasGAP317-326.
source: Thus, in HeLa cells, KCNN4 channels regulate the membrane translocation of the peptide. This was confirmed by knocking out KCNN4 in these cells (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition and genetic knockout experiments.

claim: Resistance to TAT-RasGAP317-326-induced death in KCNQ5 knock-out Raji cells and KCNN4 knock-out SKW6.4 or HeLa cells was restored through ectopic expression of the corresponding FLAG- or V5-tagged channels.
source: Resistance to TAT-RasGAP317-326-induced death in KCNQ5 knock-out Raji cells and KCNN4 knock-out SKW6.4 or HeLa cells was restored through ectopic expression of the corresponding FLAG- or V5-tagged channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-F), ruling out off-target effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiments showing restoration of sensitivity to the peptide upon re-expression of the channels.

claim: The percentage of cells with diffuse cytosolic location of FITC-TAT-RasGAP317-326 was drastically diminished in cells lacking one of the CRISPR/Cas9 screen-identified potassium channels.
source: Compared to their respective wild-type controls, the percentage of cells with diffuse cytosolic location of FITC-TAT-RasGAP317-326 was drastically diminished in cells lacking one of the CRISPR/Cas9 screen-identified potassium channels in the respective cell lines (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy quantitation showing reduced direct translocation in knockout cells.

claim: The invalidation of potassium channels did not affect transferrin or dextran internalization into cells.
source: The invalidation of potassium channels did not affect transferrin or dextran internalization into cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C) or the infectivity of vesicular stomatitis virus (Torriani et al., 2019), substantiating the non-involvement of these channels in endocytic pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing no difference in transferrin or dextran uptake between wild-type and knockout cells.

claim: The invalidation of potassium channels did not affect the infectivity of vesicular stomatitis virus.
source: The invalidation of potassium channels did not affect transferrin or dextran internalization into cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C) or the infectivity of vesicular stomatitis virus (Torriani et al., 2019), substantiating the non-involvement of these channels in endocytic pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Difference in peptide binding is not the cause of the inability of potassium channel knock-out cells to take up TAT-RasGAP317-326.
source: Difference in peptide binding is therefore not the cause of the inability of potassium channel knock-out cells to take up TAT-RasGAP317-326.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing that even at higher concentrations that achieve equivalent or higher surface binding, knockout cells still do not efficiently internalize the peptide.

claim: The luciferase activity triggered by TAT-PNA was diminished in the presence of potassium channel inhibitors and in potassium channel knock-out cell lines.
source: The luciferase activity triggered by TAT-PNA was diminished in the presence of potassium channel inhibitors and in potassium channel knock-out cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data showing reduced activity in cells with impaired potassium channel function.

claim: Switch from red to green fluorescence in the TAT-Cre/loxP-RFP-STOP-loxP-GFP system took place in wild-type Raji cells but not in the KCNQ5 knock-out cells.
source: Switch from red to green fluorescence occurs only when TAT-Cre reaches the nucleus. This took place in wild-type Raji cells but not in the KCNQ5 knock-out cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data showing differential recombination in wild-type versus knockout cells.

claim: The internalization of D-JNKI1 was completely blocked in Raji cells lacking KCNQ5.
source: The internalization of this peptide was completely blocked in Raji cells lacking KCNQ5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing no internalization of D-JNKI1 in KCNQ5 knockout Raji cells.

claim: D-JNKI1 internalization was diminished in SKW6.4 cells lacking KCNN4 and KCNK5 channels, as well as in HeLa cells lacking the KCNN4 potassium channel.
source: D-JNKI1 internalization was also diminished in SKW6.4 cells lacking KCNN4 and KCNK5 channels, as well as in HeLa cells lacking the KCNN4 potassium channel (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, middle and right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced D-JNKI1 internalization in knockout cells.

claim: Potassium is the main ion involved in setting the plasma membrane potential (Vm).
source: Potassium is the main ion involved in setting the plasma membrane potential (Vm).
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Genetic disruption or pharmacological inhibition of KCNQ5 in Raji cells led to an increase in their Vm (from –26 to –15 mV).
source: Figure 3A (left graph) shows that genetic disruption or pharmacological inhibition of KCNQ5 in Raji cells led to an increase in their Vm (from –26 to –15 mV, validated with electrophysiological recordings; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane potential measurements using DiBac4(3) and electrophysiology.

claim: A minimal increase in Vm in the KCNQ5 knock-out Raji cells practically abolished CPP internalization.
source: Surprisingly, such minimal increase in Vm in the KCNQ5 knock-out Raji cells practically abolished CPP internalization (Figure 3B, left graph), indicating that above a certain threshold, the Vm is no longer permissive for CPP direct translocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing drastically reduced CPP internalization in KCNQ5 knockout cells.

claim: A trend of increased Vm was observed when KCNN4 or KCNK5 were invalidated genetically or pharmacologically in SKW6.4 and HeLa cells.
source: In SKW6.4 and HeLa cells, Vm measurement was much more variable than in Raji cells. Nevertheless, a trend of increased Vm was observed when KCNN4 or KCNK5 were invalidated genetically or pharmacologically (Figure 3A, middle and right graphs) and this was accompanied by reduced peptide uptake (Figure 3B, middle and right graphs).
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane potential measurements and peptide internalization data.

claim: It is the Vm maintenance activity of potassium channels that is important for CPP direct translocation and not some specific features of the channels.
source: As the CRISPR/Cas9 screens performed in various cell lines identified a variety of potassium channels required for efficient CPP internalization, we conclude that it is the Vm maintenance activity of these channels that is important for CPP direct translocation and not some specific features of the channels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that different potassium channels were identified in different cell lines, suggesting a common mechanism related to Vm.

claim: Depolarizing cells with gramicidin or by increasing the extracellular concentration of potassium totally blocked cytosolic peptide acquisition into the three studied cell lines.
source: Indeed, depolarizing cells with gramicidin (Eisenman et al., 1978) (making non-specific 0.4 nm pores [Kelkar and Chattopadhyay, 2007] in cell membranes) or by increasing the extracellular concentration of potassium (dissipating the potassium gradient) totally blocked cytosolic peptide acquisition into the three studied cell lines (Figure 3B) but not peptide endocytosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and confocal microscopy data showing no cytosolic CPP signal in depolarized cells.

claim: Cellular depolarization in itself inhibits TAT-RasGAP317-326 direct translocation into the cytosol.
source: Hence, cellular depolarization in itself inhibits TAT-RasGAP317-326 direct translocation into the cytosol.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that depolarization blocks cytosolic peptide acquisition.

claim: Hyperpolarization of cells lacking CRISPR/Cas9-identified potassium channels fully restored peptide translocation.
source: Figure 3B shows that hyperpolarization of cells lacking CRISPR/Cas9-identified potassium channels fully restored peptide translocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing restored CPP internalization in knockout cells treated with valinomycin or expressing KCNJ2.

claim: Hyperpolarization increased peptide cytosolic acquisition in wild-type cells.
source: Moreover, hyperpolarization increased peptide cytosolic acquisition in wild-type cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing increased CPP internalization in wild-type cells treated with valinomycin or expressing KCNJ2.

claim: Primary rat cortical neurons that naturally have a low Vm (–48 mV) take up the CPP in their cytosol more efficiently than cells with higher Vm such as HeLa cells (–25 mV).
source: Additionally, cells such as primary rat cortical neurons that naturally have a low Vm (–48 mV) take up the CPP in their cytosol more efficiently than cells with higher Vm such as HeLa cells (–25 mV) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data comparing CPP uptake in neurons versus HeLa cells.

claim: The Vm modulates internalization of TAT-RasGAP317-326 in various cell lines.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that the Vm modulates internalization of TAT-RasGAP317-326 in various cell lines.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental results showing the relationship between Vm and CPP internalization.

claim: Depolarization, induced by either gramicidin or high extracellular potassium concentrations, led to decreased cytosolic fluorescence of TAT, R9, and Penetratin CPPs.
source: Depolarization, induced by either gramicidin or high extracellular potassium concentrations (Figure 3D), led to decreased cytosolic fluorescence of these CPPs, while valinomycin-mediated hyperpolarization favored their translocation in the cytosol (Figure 3C, upper graphs, Figure 3E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy and flow cytometry data showing reduced cytosolic CPP signal in depolarized cells.

claim: Valinomycin-mediated hyperpolarization favored translocation of TAT, R9, and Penetratin into the cytosol.
source: Depolarization, induced by either gramicidin or high extracellular potassium concentrations (Figure 3D), led to decreased cytosolic fluorescence of these CPPs, while valinomycin-mediated hyperpolarization favored their translocation in the cytosol (Figure 3C, upper graphs, Figure 3E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy and flow cytometry data showing increased cytosolic CPP signal in hyperpolarized cells.

claim: Depolarization had no impact on the ability of the cells to endocytose CPPs.
source: In contrast, depolarization had no impact on the ability of the cells to endocytose these CPPs (Figure 3C, bottom graphs), further confirming that CPP endocytosis is not affected by Vm.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing no change in the number of CPP-positive vesicles in depolarized cells.

claim: The Vm also controlled peptide translocation in non-transformed rat primary cortical neurons.
source: Although the cellular membrane composition of neurons may differ from the other cell lines used in this study, the Vm also controlled peptide translocation in non-transformed rat primary cortical neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing Vm-dependent CPP uptake in neurons.

claim: CPP membrane binding was only minimally affected by depolarization.
source: Finally, we note that CPP membrane binding was only minimally affected by depolarization (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing similar surface binding in control and depolarized cells.

claim: The reason why depolarized cells do not take up CPPs is not a consequence of reduced CPP binding to cells.
source: Hence, the reason why depolarized cells do no take up CPPs is not a consequence of reduced CPP binding to cells, confirming our earlier observation obtained with TAT-RasGAP317-326 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that CPP binding is not significantly reduced in depolarized cells, yet internalization is blocked.

claim: Direct translocation of cationic CPPs is modulated by the Vm of cells and specific potassium channels are involved in this modulation.
source: Altogether the data presented in Figure 3 show that direct translocation of cationic CPPs is modulated by the Vm of cells and that specific potassium channels are involved in this modulation.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental results presented in Figure 3.

claim: Membrane hyperpolarization was achieved by setting an ion imbalance through a net charge difference of 30 positive ions (corresponding to a Vm of ~2 V) between the intracellular and extracellular spaces in the simulations.
source: Membrane hyperpolarization was achieved by setting an ion imbalance (Delemotte et al., 2008; Gao et al., 2019; Gurtovenko and Vattulainen, 2007; Herrera and Pantano, 2009) through a net charge difference of 30 positive ions (corresponding to a Vm of ~2 V) between the intracellular and extracellular spaces.
evidence: This claim describes the computational method used to simulate membrane hyperpolarization.

claim: The use of very high Vm values, typically used in computational studies, is required to capture nanosecond occurring events.
source: The use of very high Vm values, typically used in computational studies, is required to capture nanosecond occurring events.
evidence: This claim explains the rationale for using high Vm values in simulations.

claim: CPPs approached the membrane on the extracellular side and this led to the formation of a water column within the membrane that the CPP then used to move to the intracellular space in the presence of ~2 V Vm.
source: In presence of ~2 V Vm, the CPPs approached the membrane on the extracellular side and this led to the formation of a water column within the membrane that the CPP then used to move to the intracellular space (Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The movement of the positive charges carried by the CPPs, as well as extracellular cations, to the intracellular compartment via the water pore induced membrane depolarization.
source: The movement of the positive charges carried by the CPPs, as well as extracellular cations, to the intracellular compartment via the water pore induced membrane depolarization.
evidence: This claim is based on the simulation results showing charge movement during CPP translocation.

claim: Membrane depolarization provoked the collapse of the water pore and membrane resealing.
source: This depolarization provoked the collapse of the water pore and membrane resealing.
evidence: This claim is based on the simulation results showing pore closure after CPP translocation.

claim: The mere presence of the CPP in the absence of a sufficiently low Vm was not enough to trigger water pore formation.
source: Even though CPPs play an active role in their internalization, the mere presence of the CPP in the absence of a sufficiently low Vm was not enough to trigger water pore formation (Figure 4B, right graph and Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data showing no CPP translocation at 0 V.

claim: TAT, R9, and Penetratin all translocated into the intracellular compartment but with different propensities and with different kinetics.
source: TAT, R9, and Penetratin all translocated into the intracellular compartment but with different propensities (Figure 4B, left graph) and with different kinetics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) that appeared to be related to the positive charges they carry (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A): the more positively charged a CPP, the higher probability to translocate across cell membranes and the faster kinetics of water pore formation at a given Vm.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data showing differential translocation of different CPPs.

claim: The more positively charged a CPP, the higher probability to translocate across cell membranes and the faster kinetics of water pore formation at a given Vm.
source: TAT, R9, and Penetratin all translocated into the intracellular compartment but with different propensities (Figure 4B, left graph) and with different kinetics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) that appeared to be related to the positive charges they carry (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A): the more positively charged a CPP, the higher probability to translocate across cell membranes and the faster kinetics of water pore formation at a given Vm.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between CPP charge and translocation efficiency observed in simulations.

claim: The free energy barriers recorded in depolarized membranes (Vm = 0) and polarized membranes (Vm = –80 mV) were similar.
source: The free energy barriers recorded in depolarized membranes (Vm = 0) and polarized membranes (Vm = –80 mV) were similar (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by metadynamics simulation data showing similar free energy barriers at 0 and -80 mV.

claim: The obtained value of about 200 kJ/mol for the free energy barrier is in line with recent estimation of the free energy barrier associated with CPP translocation at a Vm = 0.
source: The obtained value of about 200 kJ/mol is in line with recent estimation of the free energy barrier associated with CPP translocation at a Vm = 0 (Gao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previously published computational results.

claim: Only at much lower Vm values (–150 mV) was a marked decrease in free energy barrier recorded.
source: Only at much lower Vm values (–150 mV) was a marked decrease in free energy barrier recorded.
evidence: This claim is supported by metadynamics simulation data showing reduced free energy barrier at -150 mV.

claim: Hyperpolarization values found in resting cells (down to about –80 mV in neurons and higher in many other cells types) are not more favorable than fully depolarized membranes to establish conditions for the formation of water pores.
source: This indicates that hyperpolarization values found in resting cells (down to about –80 mV in neurons and higher in many other cells types; Yang and Brackenbury, 2013) are not more favorable than fully depolarized membranes to establish conditions for the formation of water pores.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the simulation results showing similar free energy barriers at 0 and -80 mV.

claim: Cells need to decrease their Vm to much lower values (e.g. –150 mV or lower) to reach conditions compatible with water pore formation.
source: It appears therefore that cells need to decrease their Vm to much lower values (e.g. –150 mV or lower) to reach conditions compatible with water pore formation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the simulation results showing reduced free energy barrier only at -150 mV.

claim: The presence of CPPs on the cell surface induces locally a substantial voltage drop from the resting Vm.
source: We therefore postulate that the presence of CPPs on the cell surface induces locally a substantial voltage drop from the resting Vm.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis proposed to reconcile the simulation results with the live cell observations.

claim: The presence of CPPs at the cell surface is sufficient to decrease locally the transmembrane potential to about –150 mV.
source: This simulation indicated that the presence of CPPs at the cell surface is sufficient to decrease locally the transmembrane potential to about –150 mV (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrostatic potential map calculations from simulations.

claim: CPPs further decrease the Vm of resting cells to very low values (equal to or less than –150 mV) that are compatible with spontaneous water pore formation.
source: In conclusion, our data support a model where CPPs further decrease the Vm of resting cells to very low values (equal to or less than –150 mV) that are compatible with spontaneous water pore formation and that we coin megapolarization.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the simulation and experimental data.

claim: The electric force exerted on CPPs when cells are megapolarized permits CPPs to accumulate in the cytosol and reach concentrations that are higher than in the extracellular milieu.
source: Our model also predicts that the electric force exerted on CPPs when cells are megapolarized permit CPPs to accumulate in the cytosol and reach concentrations that are higher than in the extracellular milieu.
evidence: This claim is a prediction from the model.

claim: Cells can concentrate TAT-RasGAP317-326 in the cytosol of Raji and HeLa cells, up to 100 times in extreme cases.
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 1C shows indeed that cells can concentrate TAT-RasGAP317-326 in the cytosol of Raji and HeLa cells, up to 100 times in extreme cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing higher fluorescence intensity inside cells than in the media.

claim: Propidium iodide (PI) has a diameter of 0.8–1.5 nm.
source: Propidium iodide (PI), with a diameter of 0.8–1.5 nm (Bowman et al., 2010) or fluorophore-labeled 3, 10, and 40 kDa dextrans, with diameters (provided by Thermo Fisher) of 2.3 ± 0.38 (Thorne and Nicholson, 2006), 4.5, and 8.6 nm, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), were used to estimate the size of the water pores formed in the presence of CPPs in live cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Fluorophore-labeled 3, 10, and 40 kDa dextrans have diameters of 2.3 ± 0.38, 4.5, and 8.6 nm, respectively.
source: Propidium iodide (PI), with a diameter of 0.8–1.5 nm (Bowman et al., 2010) or fluorophore-labeled 3, 10, and 40 kDa dextrans, with diameters (provided by Thermo Fisher) of 2.3 ± 0.38 (Thorne and Nicholson, 2006), 4.5, and 8.6 nm, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), were used to estimate the size of the water pores formed in the presence of CPPs in live cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by information provided by the manufacturer and a citation.

claim: PI and CPPs efficiently co-entered cells.
source: While PI and CPPs efficiently co-entered cells (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D), there was only marginal co-entry of the dextrans with the CPPs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing co-localization of PI and CPP signals in cells.

claim: There was only marginal co-entry of the dextrans with the CPPs.
source: While PI and CPPs efficiently co-entered cells (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D), there was only marginal co-entry of the dextrans with the CPPs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing low percentage of cells with dextran cytosolic staining.

claim: The marginal dextran co-entry was inversely correlated with the dextran diameters: ~2.3-nm-wide dextrans entered cells better than ~4.5-nm-wide dextrans and ~8.6-nm-wide dextrans mostly remained outside cells.
source: The marginal dextran co-entry was inversely correlated with the dextran diameters (inset in Figure 5B): ~2.3-nm-wide dextrans entered cells better than ~4.5-nm-wide dextrans and ~8.6-nm-wide dextrans mostly remained outside cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing size-dependent dextran entry.

claim: The entry of PI and CPPs in cells occurred with identical kinetics.
source: The entry of PI and CPPs in cells occurred with identical kinetics (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), further supporting the notion that they enter cells together.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data showing simultaneous increase in PI and CPP signals.

claim: The PI/CPP co-entry was prevented by cell depolarization.
source: The PI/CPP co-entry was prevented by cell depolarization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which is expected if PI accesses the cytosol via the megapolarization-induced pores used by CPP to enter cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing no PI entry in depolarized cells.

claim: CPPs do not need to be labeled with a fluorophore to allow PI co-entry into cells.
source: CPPs do not need to be labeled with a fluorophore to allow PI co-entry into cells (Figure 5B, 'unlabeled TAT+ PI' condition), ruling out phototoxicity as a confounding effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing PI entry with unlabeled TAT.

claim: Water pores triggered by CPPs allow molecules up to ~2 nm in diameter to efficiently enter cells.
source: These data are compatible with the notion that water pores triggered by CPPs allow molecules up to ~2 nm in diameter to efficiently enter cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-entry experiments showing efficient PI entry but limited dextran entry.

claim: Molecules in the 2–5 nm diameter range, such as 3 and 10 kDa dextrans, can still use this entry route to a limited extent.
source: They are also in line with the in silico prediction of the water pore diameter of 1.6±0.26 nm obtained by analyzing the structure of the pore at the transition state (i.e. when the CPP is crossing the cell membrane; see Figure 4A). Molecules in the 2–5 nm diameter range, such as 3 and 10 kDa dextrans, can still use this entry route to a limited extent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-entry experiments showing limited entry of 3 and 10 kDa dextrans.

claim: The Cre recombinase, with a diameter of 5 nm, can be transported by TAT into cells.
source: In this context, the Cre recombinase, with a diameter of 5 nm (estimated from its crystal structure; NDB:PD0003), can be transported by TAT into cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), another indication that the pores used by cationic CPPs to enter cells can allow the passage of molecules up to 5 nm.
evidence: This claim is supported by the TAT-Cre recombination assay showing functional Cre delivery.

claim: The in silico prediction of the water pore diameter is 1.6±0.26 nm.
source: They are also in line with the in silico prediction of the water pore diameter of 1.6±0.26 nm obtained by analyzing the structure of the pore at the transition state (i.e. when the CPP is crossing the cell membrane; see Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of the pore structure during CPP translocation.

claim: K9 peptide made of nine lysine residues was less capable of translocating into cells compared to R9.
source: Despite identical net positive charges (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), and as reported earlier (Mitchell et al., 2000), the K9 peptide made of nine lysine residues was less capable of translocating into cells compared to R9 (Figure 5B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, right graph).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing reduced K9 internalization compared to R9.

claim: When cells have taken up K9, PI co-internalized as well.
source: However, in the few cases when cells have taken up K9, PI co-internalized as well (middle graph of Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing PI entry in cells that took up K9.

claim: K9 has a reduced capacity compared to R9 to trigger water pore formation but when they do, PI can efficiently translocate through the pores created by K9.
source: This indicates that K9 has a reduced capacity compared to R9 to trigger water pore formation but when they do, PI can efficiently translocate through the pores created by K9.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that K9 enters cells less efficiently than R9, but when it does, PI co-enters.

claim: The hyperpolarizing drug valinomycin significantly increased PI cell permeability.
source: Figure 5D (left) shows that the hyperpolarizing drug valinomycin significantly increased PI cell permeability.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing increased PI cytosolic fluorescence in valinomycin-treated cells.

claim: Depolarization, mediated by gramicidin, reduced PI internalization.
source: In contrast, depolarization, mediated by gramicidin, reduced PI internalization (Figure 5D, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing reduced PI cytosolic fluorescence in gramicidin-treated cells.

claim: Cells incubated with CPPs took up PI in their cytosol to a much greater extent than when cells were treated with valinomycin.
source: Cells incubated with CPPs took up PI in their cytosol to a much greater extent than when cells were treated with valinomycin (Figure 5D, left), as expected if CPPs participate in setting plasma membrane megapolarization.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing higher PI cytosolic fluorescence in CPP-treated cells compared to valinomycin-treated cells.

claim: The Vm of cells incubated with a CPP was estimated to be in the order of –150 mV based on the correlation between cytosolic PI accumulation and Vm.
source: Figure 5E shows the correlation between cytosolic PI accumulation over time and Vm. Based on this correlation, we estimated the Vm of cells incubated with a CPP to be in the order of –150 mV (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by calculations based on the correlation between PI fluorescence and Vm.

claim: Water pore formation in cells is favored by cell hyperpolarization and inhibited by depolarization.
source: In accordance with the modeling experiments, these data further support the notion (i) that water pore formation in cells is favored by cell hyperpolarization and inhibited by depolarization and (ii) that CPPs themselves (Rao et al., 2014; Wallbrecher et al., 2017) further contribute to the establishment of local megapolarization in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the PI co-entry experiments and modeling data.

claim: CPPs themselves further contribute to the establishment of local megapolarization in the plasma membrane.
source: In accordance with the modeling experiments, these data further support the notion (i) that water pore formation in cells is favored by cell hyperpolarization and inhibited by depolarization and (ii) that CPPs themselves (Rao et al., 2014; Wallbrecher et al., 2017) further contribute to the establishment of local megapolarization in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the PI co-entry experiments and modeling data, with supporting citations.

claim: Systemic exposure of zebrafish embryos to valinomycin in Egg water led to cell hyperpolarization and improved internalization of a TAT-based CPP.
source: Systemic exposure of zebrafish embryos to valinomycin in Egg water led to cell hyperpolarization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and improved internalization of a TAT-based CPP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments in zebrafish showing increased CPP uptake with valinomycin treatment.

claim: Systemic valinomycin treatment in zebrafish, while not acutely toxic, halted development.
source: This systemic treatment, while not acutely toxic, halted development (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by viability and developmental assessment data in zebrafish.

claim: Local valinomycin injection in zebrafish did not affect long-term viability and efficiently increased CPP cellular internalization.
source: However, local valinomycin injection did not affect long-term viability (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) and efficiently increased CPP cellular internalization (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments in zebrafish showing increased CPP uptake with local valinomycin injection without affecting survival.

claim: Subcutaneous injections of valinomycin in mice induced tissue hyperpolarization and boosted the CPP delivery in skin cells.
source: Subcutaneous injections of valinomycin in mice induced tissue hyperpolarization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) and boosted the CPP delivery in skin cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experiments in mice showing increased CPP uptake with valinomycin treatment.

claim: Hyperpolarizing drugs can be used to ameliorate CPP internalization in animal tissues.
source: These results demonstrate that hyperpolarizing drugs can be used to ameliorate CPP internalization in animal tissues.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo experiments in zebrafish and mice.

claim: Valinomycin at the concentrations used to induce hyperpolarization (10 μM) would be lethal if systemically injected in mice (LD50 in the low micromolar range).
source: For example, valinomycin at the concentrations used to induce hyperpolarization (10 μM) would be lethal if systemically injected in mice (LD50 in the low micromolar range; Daoud and Juliano, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on valinomycin toxicity.

claim: Local administration of valinomycin is far less toxic.
source: On the other hand, local administration of valinomycin is far less toxic (Gad et al., 1985; Waksman, 1953) as confirmed here in zebrafish and mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and the in vivo experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hyperpolarizing agents may be preferentially used for local or topical applications.
source: Hyperpolarizing agents may therefore be preferentially used for local or topical applications, which is incidentally the case for the clinically approved CPPs (Abes et al., 2007; Abraham et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is a recommendation based on the toxicity considerations and is supported by citations.

claim: Water pores are created by a combination of lipid head group reorientation coupled to intrusion of a column of water in the membrane bilayer.
source: Water pores are created by a combination of lipid head group reorientation coupled to intrusion of a column of water in the membrane bilayer.
evidence: This claim is based on the simulation results showing the mechanism of water pore formation.

claim: Water movement plays an active role in the formation of the pore and is not merely occurring once the pores are formed.
source: Water movement plays therefore an active role in the formation of the pore and is not merely occurring once the pores are formed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the simulation results showing water intrusion during pore formation.

claim: The movement of the positive charges carried by the CPPs into the cell, as well as the transport of extracellular cations (e.g. Na+), dissipates the Vm, resulting in the collapse of the water pores and sealing of the plasma membrane.
source: The movement of the positive charges carried by the CPPs into the cell, as well as the transport of extracellular cations (e.g. Na+), dissipates the Vm, resulting in the collapse of the water pores and sealing of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on the simulation results showing pore closure after charge movement.

claim: CPP-mediated formation of water pores is transient and does not affect cell viability.
source: CPP-mediated formation of water pores is therefore transient and does not affect cell viability.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that cells can take up CPPs without dying (unless the CPP itself is toxic like TAT-RasGAP317-326).

claim: Multiple rounds of CPP-driven water pore formation and CPP translocation into cells can lead to intracellular accumulation of the CPP to concentrations higher than found outside cells.
source: Multiple rounds of CPP-driven water pore formation and CPP translocation into cells can lead to intracellular accumulation of the CPP to concentrations higher than found outside cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing higher CPP concentrations inside cells than in the media.

claim: Using an indirect calculation mode based on the uptake of PI alongside CPPs, the Vm required for water pores to be formed was estimated to be in the order of –150 mV.
source: Using an indirect calculation mode based on the uptake of PI alongside CPPs, we have estimated that a Vm in the order of –150 mV is required for water pores to be formed (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by calculations based on the correlation between PI fluorescence and Vm.

claim: The local Vm where CPPs interact with the plasma membranes might be much lower than –150 mV and/or changes in CPP structures occur (e.g. refolding, aggregation) leading to further reduction in free energy barrier.
source: Possibly therefore, the local Vm where CPPs interact with the plasma membranes is much lower than –150 mV and/or changes in CPP structures occur (e.g. refolding, aggregation) leading to further reduction in free energy barrier.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the observation that the free energy barrier at -150 mV is not fully abrogated.

claim: The applied coarse-grained MARTINI force field has a number of known limitations such as the chemical and spatial resolution, which are both limited compared to atomistic models.
source: It is worth mentioning that the applied coarse-grained MARTINI force field, as any other model, has a number of known limitations (Marrink et al., 2019; Marrink and Tieleman, 2013) such as the chemical and spatial resolution, which are both limited compared to atomistic models.
evidence: This claim acknowledges the limitations of the computational method used, with citations.

claim: There is a shifted balance between entropy and enthalpy in the MARTINI force field due to the reduced number of degrees of freedom.
source: There is also a shifted balance between entropy and enthalpy due to the reduced number of degrees of freedom.
evidence: This claim describes a known limitation of the MARTINI force field.

claim: The secondary structure is an input parameter of the MARTINI model, which implies that secondary structure elements remain fixed during the simulation.
source: Moreover, the secondary structure is an input parameter of the model, which implies that secondary structure elements remain fixed during the simulation (Monticelli et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim describes a known limitation of the MARTINI force field, with a citation.

claim: The coarse-grained approach has provided reliable results in the context of protein-membrane interactions and peptide translocation.
source: However, the coarse-grained approach has provided reliable results in the context of protein-membrane interactions and peptide translocation (Castillo et al., 2013; Koch et al., 2019; Marrink et al., 2003; Monticelli et al., 2008; Monticelli et al., 2010; Periole et al., 2009; Periole et al., 2007; Ramadurai et al., 2010; Yesylevskyy et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work validating the MARTINI force field.

claim: The ability of MARTINI coarse-grained force field to model realistic and heterogeneous membranes has been repeatedly reported in literature.
source: Moreover, the ability of MARTINI coarse-grained force field to model realistic and heterogeneous membranes has been repeatedly reported in literature, as summarized in a recent review paper (Marrink et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review paper.

claim: The number of positively charged amino acids influences the ability of CPPs to hyperpolarize cells and hence to form water pores that they take to translocate into cells.
source: Our model posits that the number of positively charged amino acids influence the ability of CPPs to hyperpolarize cells and hence to form water pores that they take to translocate into cells.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the simulation and experimental data showing charge-dependent CPP translocation.

claim: CPP hydropathy strongly correlates with penetration of water molecules in the lipid bilayer.
source: CPP hydropathy strongly correlates with penetration of water molecules in the lipid bilayer, thus supporting the hypothesis that the amount of water each CPP can route inside the membrane is modulated by the hydrophobic and hydrophilic character of the peptide (Grasso et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The nature of cationic amino acids in peptides determines their translocation abilities.
source: The nature of cationic amino acids in peptides determines their translocation abilities.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that arginine-rich peptides translocate better than lysine-rich peptides.

claim: Peptides made of nine lysines (K9) poorly reach the cytosol.
source: It is known for example that peptides made of nine lysines (K9) poorly reaches the cytosol (Figure 5B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) and that replacing arginine by lysine in Penetratin significantly diminishes its internalization (Amand et al., 2012; Mitchell et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: Replacing arginine by lysine in Penetratin significantly diminishes its internalization.
source: It is known for example that peptides made of nine lysines (K9) poorly reaches the cytosol (Figure 5B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) and that replacing arginine by lysine in Penetratin significantly diminishes its internalization (Amand et al., 2012; Mitchell et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Once embedded into membranes, lysine residues tend to lose protons.
source: However, it has been determined that, once embedded into membranes, lysine residues tend to lose protons (Armstrong et al., 2016; Li et al., 2013; MacCallum et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Lysine deprotonation in membranes will dissipate the strong membrane potential required for the formation of water pores and prevent lysine-containing CPPs to cross the membrane.
source: This will thus dissipate the strong membrane potential required for the formation of water pores and prevent lysine-containing CPPs to cross the membrane.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that lysine residues lose protons in membranes.

claim: Arginine residues are not deprotonated in membranes and water pores can therefore be maintained allowing the arginine-rich CPPs to be taken up by cells.
source: In contrast, arginine residues are not deprotonated in membranes and water pores can therefore be maintained allowing the arginine-rich CPPs to be taken up by cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that arginine-rich CPPs translocate better than lysine-rich CPPs.

claim: Arginine can form two hydrogen bonds while lysine can only form one.
source: An additional potential explanation for the internalization differences observed between arginine- and lysine-rich peptides is that even though both arginine and lysine are basic amino acids, they differ in their ability to form hydrogen bonds, the guanidinium group of arginine being able to form two hydrogen bonds (Fromm et al., 1995) while the lysyl group of lysine can only form one.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Compared to lysine, arginine would form more stable electrostatic interactions with the plasma membrane.
source: Compared to lysine, arginine would therefore form more stable electrostatic interactions with the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the difference in hydrogen bonding capacity between arginine and lysine.

claim: The optimal length of consecutive arginine residues appears to be between 9 and 16 amino acids, resulting in optimal CPP cytosolic acquisition.
source: According to previously published studies (Kosuge et al., 2008; Mitchell et al., 2000), the optimal length of consecutive arginine residues appears to be between 9 and 16 amino acids, resulting in optimal CPP cytosolic acquisition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Shorter and longer polyarginine peptides have decreased internalization efficiencies.
source: Shorter and longer peptides have decreased internalization efficiencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The role of the Vm presented in the model is consistent with the reduced uptake of short polyarginine peptides.
source: The role of the Vm presented in our model is consistent with the reduced uptake of short polyarginine peptides but the Vm parameter of our model cannot explain why longer polyarginine peptides are less efficiently taken up by cells.
evidence: This claim is an assessment of the model's explanatory power.

claim: The Vm parameter of the model cannot explain why longer polyarginine peptides are less efficiently taken up by cells.
source: The role of the Vm presented in our model is consistent with the reduced uptake of short polyarginine peptides but the Vm parameter of our model cannot explain why longer polyarginine peptides are less efficiently taken up by cells.
evidence: This claim is an assessment of the model's limitations.

claim: The water pores created by megapolarization have a diameter of about 2 (–5) nm.
source: Our work however also indicates that the water pores created by megapolarization have a diameter of about 2 (–5) nm.
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-entry experiments with molecules of different sizes.

claim: Molecules larger than 2 nm are less efficiently transported through water pores.
source: Molecules larger than 2 nm are therefore less efficiently transported through these water pores and if polyarginine peptides reach that size their internalization will be hindered.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-entry experiments showing size-dependent entry.

claim: The efficiency of direct translocation of peptides is likely modulated by their sizes, the secondary structures they adopt, and the number of positive charges they carry.
source: The efficiency of direct translocation of peptides is therefore likely modulated by their sizes, the secondary structures they adopt, and the number of positive charges they carry.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the various observations about factors affecting CPP translocation.

claim: Cationic residues are not the only determinant in CPP direct translocation.
source: Cationic residues are not the only determinant in CPP direct translocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that tryptophan residues also play important roles.

claim: The presence of tryptophan residues plays important roles in the ability of CPPs to cross cellular membranes.
source: The presence of tryptophan residues also plays important roles in the ability of CPPs to cross cellular membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that Penetratin, with only three arginines but containing tryptophans, translocates efficiently.

claim: Penetratin, despite only bearing three arginine residues, can penetrate cells with similar propensities compared to R9 or TAT that contain 9 and 8 arginine residues, respectively.
source: This can be inferred from the observation that Penetratin, despite only bearing three arginine residues, can penetrate cells with similar propensities compared to R9 or TAT that contain 9 and 8 arginine residues, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing similar translocation efficiencies of Penetratin, R9, and TAT.

claim: The aromatic characteristics of tryptophan is not sufficient to explain how it favors direct translocation.
source: The aromatic characteristics of tryptophan is not sufficient to explain how it favors direct translocation as replacing tryptophan with the aromatic amino acid phenylalanine decreases the translocation potency of the RW9 (RRWWRRWRR) CPP (Derossi et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Differences in the direct translocation promoting activities of tryptophan and phenylalanine residues may come from the higher lipid bilayer insertion capability of tryptophan compared to phenylalanine.
source: Rather, differences in the direct translocation promoting activities of tryptophan and phenylalanine residues may come from the higher lipid bilayer insertion capability of tryptophan compared to phenylalanine (Christiaens et al., 2002; Jobin et al., 2015; MacCallum et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There is a certain degree of interchangeability between arginine and tryptophan residues.
source: There is a certain degree of interchangeability between arginine and tryptophan residues as demonstrated by the fact that replacing up to four arginine residues with tryptophan amino acids in the R9 CPP preserves its ability to enter cells (Walrant et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Despite the importance of the membrane potential for CPP direct translocation into cells, other factors also appear to play a role in this process.
source: Therefore, despite the importance of the membrane potential for CPP direct translocation into cells, other factors also appear to play a role in this process.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the observations about the roles of tryptophan and other factors.

claim: The composition of the plasma membrane could modulate how CPPs translocate into cells.
source: While the nature of the CPPs likely dictate their uptake efficiency as discussed in the previous paragraph, the composition of the plasma membrane could also modulate how CPPs translocate into cells.
evidence: This claim is speculation about potential factors affecting CPP translocation.

claim: Cancer cells display abnormal plasma membrane composition.
source: But as cancer cells display abnormal plasma membrane composition (Szlasa et al., 2020), it will be of interest in the future to determine how important this is for their capacity to take up CPPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Hyperpolarization induced by drugs such as valinomycin represents a simple alternative or parallel approach to optimize CPP internalization.
source: We propose, based on the work described here, that hyperpolarization induced by drugs such as valinomycin represents a simple alternative or parallel approach to optimize CPP internalization.
evidence: This claim is a proposal based on the experimental results.

claim: Hyperpolarizing drugs may be toxic when systemically applied.
source: However, hyperpolarizing drugs may be toxic when systemically applied.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that systemic valinomycin treatment halted zebrafish development and by citations about valinomycin toxicity.

claim: The molecular characterization of the process of CPP direct translocation can be taken advantage of to improve or optimize 'old' CPPs.
source: Our molecular characterization of the process of CPP direct translocation can be taken advantage of to (i) improve or optimize 'old' CPPs, (ii) design new CPPs, (iii) help explain the behavior of newly discovered CPPs (Du et al., 2011; Kauffman et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2009), (iv) discriminate between target cells and cells that should be left unaffected based on Vm, and (v) distinguish between direct translocation and endosomal escape.
evidence: This claim is a proposal for future applications of the work.

claim: The molecular characterization of the process of CPP direct translocation can be taken advantage of to design new CPPs.
source: Our molecular characterization of the process of CPP direct translocation can be taken advantage of to (i) improve or optimize 'old' CPPs, (ii) design new CPPs, (iii) help explain the behavior of newly discovered CPPs (Du et al., 2011; Kauffman et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2009), (iv) discriminate between target cells and cells that should be left unaffected based on Vm, and (v) distinguish between direct translocation and endosomal escape.
evidence: This claim is a proposal for future applications of the work.

claim: The molecular characterization of the process of CPP direct translocation can be taken advantage of to help explain the behavior of newly discovered CPPs.
source: Our molecular characterization of the process of CPP direct translocation can be taken advantage of to (i) improve or optimize 'old' CPPs, (ii) design new CPPs, (iii) help explain the behavior of newly discovered CPPs (Du et al., 2011; Kauffman et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2009), (iv) discriminate between target cells and cells that should be left unaffected based on Vm, and (v) distinguish between direct translocation and endosomal escape.
evidence: This claim is a proposal for future applications of the work, with citations to examples of newly discovered CPPs.

claim: The molecular characterization of the process of CPP direct translocation can be taken advantage of to discriminate between target cells and cells that should be left unaffected based on Vm.
source: Our molecular characterization of the process of CPP direct translocation can be taken advantage of to (i) improve or optimize 'old' CPPs, (ii) design new CPPs, (iii) help explain the behavior of newly discovered CPPs (Du et al., 2011; Kauffman et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2009), (iv) discriminate between target cells and cells that should be left unaffected based on Vm, and (v) distinguish between direct translocation and endosomal escape.
evidence: This claim is a proposal for future applications of the work.

claim: The molecular characterization of the process of CPP direct translocation can be taken advantage of to distinguish between direct translocation and endosomal escape.
source: Our molecular characterization of the process of CPP direct translocation can be taken advantage of to (i) improve or optimize 'old' CPPs, (ii) design new CPPs, (iii) help explain the behavior of newly discovered CPPs (Du et al., 2011; Kauffman et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2009), (iv) discriminate between target cells and cells that should be left unaffected based on Vm, and (v) distinguish between direct translocation and endosomal escape.
evidence: This claim is a proposal for future applications of the work.

claim: The impact on megapolarization should be evaluated when chemical modifications are performed on cationic CPPs to augment their delivery capacities.
source: The present work indicates that the impact on megapolarization should be evaluated when chemical modifications are performed on cationic CPPs to augment their delivery capacities.
evidence: This claim is a recommendation based on the findings of the work.
